name: Moving bits instead of watts: Accelerating global AI data-centre deployment at the energy-digital-water-land nexus
headline: Moving bits instead of watts: Accelerating global AI data-centre deployment at the energy-digital-water-land nexus
abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving an unprecedented expansion of data centres. However, this growth is increasingly stalled by grid transmission constraints that trap new data centres in years-long connection queues. Unlike electricity, computation can be moved across the globe through fibre-optic networks, but whether this spatial transfer can bypass constrained grids and accelerate global AI data-centre deployment remains unknown. Here we develop a global framework that places future data-centre capacity in energy-abundant regions and routes computational workloads through fibre-optic networks rather than transmitting electricity. We evaluate the framework through more than 11 million hourly operation simulations at subnational resolution, integrating constraints on energy systems, water, digital connectivity, land and financing risk. Results show that across multiple data-centre development and climate-policy scenarios, leveraging global data transfer allows new data centres to be sited where these conditions are favourable, lowering construction costs by 44-47% and carbon emissions by 38%. By treating the global fibre-optic network as an energy-system asset, it avoids 34-67 GW of high-voltage transmission capacity, comparable in magnitude to Italy's national peak electricity demand. Crucially, this methodology could bring more than 95% of connection-delayed data centres online in 2030, with Canada, the Nordic countries and the Arabian Peninsula emerging as preferred locations for data-centre development. Our findings establish computational mobility as an alternative to energy-system expansion, informing the coordinated global development of energy and artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

description: Qu et al. (2026), arXiv:2610.35088, investigate AI data center grid interconnection bottlenecks through geographic workload shifting and data center siting optimization. Their approach places new computing capacity in resource-suitable regions and serves distant demand through fiber-optic networks. It jointly considers energy infrastructure, renewable energy potential, cooling water, land, digital connectivity, financing and workload latency. This is a global capacity-planning study across 149 countries, with construction-cost estimates for more than 4,000 subnational regions. In modeled 2030 scenarios, computation-transfer siting could connect more than 95% of otherwise delayed capacity. The reported comparison estimates 37.9% lower annual CO₂ emissions from new capacity, including data transmission. Results depend on scenario assumptions and receiving locations; the study does not demonstrate a deployed real-time workload router.

about.name: Grid interconnection bottlenecks; grid connection queues
about.description: Delayed connection of new data center capacity under electricity-infrastructure constraints. The model compares local energy expansion with locating new capacity elsewhere.

about.name: Geographic workload shifting; spatial load shifting; computational mobility
about.description: Serving demand from a different geographic location through fiber networks. Here the central decision is where to build new capacity, rather than live migration between existing facilities.

about.name: Data center siting optimization; energy-water-land nexus
about.description: Joint constrained optimization of energy supply, water, land, digital connectivity and finance. Multiple siting criteria enter a cost-and-constraint model; this is not a standalone multicriteria ranking method.

about.name: Carbon-aware workload scheduling; renewable-energy integration
about.description: Related applications of flexible computation. This study evaluates infrastructure planning and route-dependent emissions; it does not provide a real-time carbon-aware scheduler.
